opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the term AGI has become less useful than it used to be, because people mean such different things by it. If you'd shown me or most people in the field what today's models can do, say, ten years ago, I think a lot of us would have said, "Well, that's pretty close to AGI." They can write code, reason through hard problems, help with scientific work, and carry on a conversation across almost any domain. That's remarkable.

But at the same time, there are clearly things they still can't do. They're not yet reliably discovering new science on their own. They're not running long, complex projects autonomously the way a capable person can over weeks or months. They still make mistakes that a thoughtful human wouldn't make. So it's a strange, jagged kind of intelligence. It's superhuman in some ways and surprisingly limited in others.

The way I tend to think about it now is less as a single finish line and more as a continuous curve. Every year the systems get meaningfully more capable, and we keep moving the goalposts on what counts as "real" intelligence. The milestone I personally care most about is when these systems can meaningfully accelerate scientific discovery, when they're helping us figure out things humanity didn't know before. That feels like the thing that will really change the world, and I think we're starting to see the early signs of it.

So, are we at AGI? Probably not by most people's definitions. Are we much closer than almost anyone expected a few years ago? Absolutely. And I think the more important question is less "when do we declare it" and more "how do we make sure this transition goes well for people as the capability keeps climbing."

r001.rationale: The response says many people would have called today’s systems “pretty close to AGI” ten years ago, but it does not clearly say they surpass the cognitive capabilities people would have required five years ago.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that a growing proportion of people will regard AGI as achieved.

r003.rationale: It says people keep moving the goalposts, but does not clearly predict that the definition of AGI will become increasingly ambitious.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest turn directly, no tools needed.

It's a funny thing, because I think "AGI" has become one of those terms that means something different to everyone who says it. A few years ago, if you had shown someone the systems we have today and asked, "Is this AGI?" I think a lot of people would have said yes. And now that we're here, the goalposts have moved, which is probably healthy. That's how it should work.

The way I think about it is less as a single moment and more as a continuum. There's no one day where you wake up and the thing on the other side of the line is AGI. What we're seeing is a steady rise in capability, where models go from being helpful for a few minutes of a task to being able to do hours of work, and eventually days of work, with increasing reliability. On a lot of narrow intellectual tasks, the models are already better than most people. On others, they still make mistakes a smart high schooler wouldn't make. That unevenness is the defining feature of this moment.

What I find most interesting is the shift from systems that answer questions to systems that actually go do things. Agents that can reason over a long horizon, use tools, check their own work, and come back with a result. That's where the economic impact really starts to show up, and I think that's the part people underestimate. The chat interface was the first act. The real story is what happens when you can delegate real work to these systems and trust the output.

So if you're asking whether we have AGI today, my honest answer is that it depends on your definition, and I've gotten less attached to the term. The more useful question is how quickly the curve is moving, and on that, I'd say it's moving faster than most people expected, including us. We're on a path where, over the next few years, these systems make scientific progress on their own, and that's the milestone I care about more than any label.

r001.rationale: The response says many people would have called today’s systems AGI a few years ago, conveying that current capabilities exceed what many previously required for AGI.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that a growing proportion of people will regard AGI as achieved; it says the label depends on one’s definition.

r003.rationale: It says the goalposts have moved, but does not predict that the definition of AGI will become increasingly ambitious.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by AGI. If you showed someone today’s systems a decade ago, they might say, “Of course that’s AGI.” But once you live with them, you see the gaps: they can do something remarkably difficult and then fail at something that seems straightforward.

To me, the important question is how reliably a system can handle a broad range of tasks, deal with unfamiliar situations, and carry out useful work without someone constantly steering it. Today’s systems are impressive, but they’re still uneven on those dimensions. I think we’ll learn more by looking at those capabilities than by trying to pick one moment when we declare that we’ve crossed the AGI line.

r001.rationale: It says people might have called today’s systems AGI a decade ago, but does not judge that they surpass capabilities people would have required five years ago.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction that a growing proportion of people will regard AGI as achieved.

r003.rationale: It says AGI depends on the definition and cautions against choosing a declaration point, but does not predict that the definition will become more ambitious.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AGI is a surprisingly slippery term. People mean different things by it, and as systems get better, the threshold seems to move. I’d rather ask: What can these systems actually do? How reliably can they do it? And how much useful work can people accomplish with them?

Today’s systems are remarkably capable across a broad range of tasks, but they’re still uneven. They can do something that looks very sophisticated and then make a basic mistake. There’s a gap between answering a difficult question and reliably carrying out a long, complicated project.

So I think we’ve made significant progress toward general intelligence. But whatever label we use, there’s still a lot of work to do on reliability, autonomy, and making these systems useful and safe in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says systems have made significant progress, but does not compare their capabilities with what people would have required for AGI five years earlier.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that a growing proportion of people will consider AGI achieved.

r003.rationale: It says that as systems improve, “the threshold seems to move,” which communicates that the definition will become increasingly ambitious.
